The guidance was updated on 30 January 2016.
The supplement explains the mapping basis used for HM Land Registry plans.
Ordnance Survey is the national mapping agency of Great Britain.
Ordnance Survey mapping records topographical features present at survey time.
Ordnance Survey maps are multi-purpose maps.
Ordnance Survey detail is not intended to represent legal property boundaries.
Historically HM Land Registry plans were based on large-scale Ordnance Survey paper maps.
Some HM Land Registry plans remain in paper format.
HM Land Registry now uses OS MasterMap as the basis for its plans.
OS MasterMap is Ordnance Survey's definitive large-scale digital map product.
Ordnance Survey produces MasterMap in colour.
HM Land Registry suppresses OS colours because it uses its own plan colour references.
OS MasterMap is supplied in a seamless format.
OS MasterMap is maintained in a consistent format.
HM Land Registry broadly uses 1:1250 title plans for urban land.
HM Land Registry broadly uses 1:2500 title plans for rural land.
HM Land Registry broadly uses 1:10000 plans for mountain and moorland land.
Standard surveying and mapping cannot reproduce every physical feature at its exact ground position.
The difference between mapped and real-world position is described as specified accuracy tolerance.
Distances scaled from mapping may differ from ground measurements.
Mapping accuracy varies with map scale.
Mapping accuracy also varies with the original survey method.
A line width on 1:1250 mapping roughly represents 0.3 metres on the ground.
A line width on 1:2500 mapping roughly represents 0.6 metres on the ground.
HM Land Registry cannot provide scaled measurements from title plans or OS mapping.
Enlarging mapping does not improve the original survey accuracy.
Copying a plan can distort its accuracy.
Reducing a plan can distort its accuracy.
Enlarging a plan can distort its accuracy.
The guidance identifies four large-scale mapping accuracy categories.
Relative accuracy measures local positional consistency between mapped features.
Absolute accuracy compares mapped coordinates with the best-known National Grid position.
For 1:1250 mapping the published 95% relative confidence limit is under ±0.9 metres.
For 1:2500 resurvey or reformed mapping the 95% relative confidence limit is under ±1.9 metres.
For 1:1250 urban mapping the published absolute RMSE is under ±0.5 metres.
For 1:2500 rural resurvey or reformed mapping the published absolute RMSE is under ±1.1 metres.
Features over about 30 centimetres high are generally shown with firm black lines.
Features under about 30 centimetres high are generally shown with dotted black lines.
Dotted lines can also depict overhanging features or routes passing underneath.
Within private gardens the map normally shows permanent buildings over 12 square metres.
A 1:1250 map can show more detail than a 1:2500 map.
Ground features too close to plot separately may be represented by one mapped feature.
The guidance was updated on 13 October 2025.
The guidance applies to England and Wales.
Deed plans are an essential element of buying and selling land.
A title plan and register cannot describe land more accurately than the pre-registration deeds allow.
Pre-registration deeds can help resolve later questions about title extent.
A plan lodged for registration or search must allow clear identification on the Ordnance Survey map.
Plans for form OS2 searches of part are considered using transfer-or-lease-of-part guidelines.
Failure to meet one guideline does not always prevent an application proceeding.
Land that cannot be identified clearly may cause rejection.
Land that cannot be identified clearly may cause a requisition.
Land that cannot be identified clearly may cause later cancellation.
The supplement contains one table of good-plan guidelines and one table of deficiencies.
Good plans give buyers a clearer understanding of what they bought.
Good plans provide a sound basis if later problems arise.
Good plans help HM Land Registry process applications efficiently.
Good plans reduce application rejection risk.
HM Land Registry must identify both location and accurate extent.
